M1 · Special Functions for Scattering

Learning goals. After this chapter you should be able to

  • separate the Schrödinger equation in spherical coordinates and explain why angular momentum is
    quantized;
  • use Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics: recurrences, orthogonality, parity, the
    addition theorem and the large-lll asymptotic form;
  • work with the spherical Bessel, Neumann and Hankel functions and their Riccati forms, and know
    when their asymptotic forms may be used;
  • expand a plane wave in partial waves and estimate how many terms are needed;
  • handle the Gamma function of complex argument and compute the Coulomb phase shift safely;
  • recognise Coulomb wave functions as confluent hypergeometric functions, with their logarithmic
    phase, turning point and penetration factor;
  • know where Airy and cylindrical Bessel functions appear in scattering;
  • evaluate all of these stably: recurrence direction, Miller’s algorithm, continued fractions and
    Steed’s method.

Prerequisites: calculus with series and ordinary differential equations, complex numbers, and
separation of variables for the hydrogen atom.

Sources: C&H §2.1 and §3.2–3.4; the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF),
chapters 5, 9, 10, 13, 14 and 33; Barnett (1981) for Steed’s method. Longer derivations are collected
in the section Detailed derivation at the end of the chapter.

How to read this chapter. Every scattering calculation in these notes is built from the
functions below. You do not need to memorize the formulas, but you should know what each function
looks like, which limits it obeys, and how a computer evaluates it reliably. The notebook checks
every identity quoted here numerically.

M1.1 Separation of variables in spherical coordinates

M0 treated scattering on a line. Real collisions happen in three dimensions, but when the potential
V(r)V(r)V(r) depends only on the distance between the two particles, the problem is spherically symmetric
and spherical coordinates (r,θ,ϕ)(r, \theta, \phi)(r,θ,ϕ) are the natural choice. In them the Laplacian reads

∇2=1r2∂∂r(r2∂∂r)+1r2sin⁡θ∂∂θ(sin⁡θ∂∂θ)+1r2sin⁡2θ∂2∂ϕ2.(M1.1)\nabla^2 = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\phi^2}. \tag{M1.1} ∇2=r21​∂r∂​(r2∂r∂​)+r2sinθ1​∂θ∂​(sinθ∂θ∂​)+r2sin2θ1​∂ϕ2∂2​.(M1.1)

The first term acts only on rrr. The other two act only on the angles, and they have a meaning of their
own: writing the angular-momentum operator L=−iℏ r×∇\mathbf{L} = -i\hbar\,\mathbf{r}\times\nablaL=−iℏr×∇ in spherical
coordinates (the standard calculation done for the hydrogen atom) gives

L2=−ℏ2[1sin⁡θ∂∂θ(sin⁡θ∂∂θ)+1sin⁡2θ∂2∂ϕ2],(M1.2)\mathbf{L}^2 = -\hbar^2\left[\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\right) + \frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\phi^2}\right], \tag{M1.2} L2=−ℏ2[sinθ1​∂θ∂​(sinθ∂θ∂​)+sin2θ1​∂ϕ2∂2​],(M1.2)

so the angular part of ∇2\nabla^2∇2 is exactly −L2/(ℏ2r2)-\mathbf{L}^2/(\hbar^2r^2)−L2/(ℏ2r2). The Schrödinger equation for a
central potential,

−ℏ22μ[1r2∂∂r(r2∂ψ∂r)−L2ψℏ2r2]+V(r) ψ=E ψ,-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\left[\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial r}\right) - \frac{\mathbf{L}^2\psi}{\hbar^2r^2}\right] + V(r)\,\psi = E\,\psi , −2μℏ2​[r21​∂r∂​(r2∂r∂ψ​)−ℏ2r2L2ψ​]+V(r)ψ=Eψ,

therefore separates. We try ψ=R(r) Θ(θ) Φ(ϕ)\psi = R(r)\,\Theta(\theta)\,\Phi(\phi)ψ=R(r)Θ(θ)Φ(ϕ) and multiply by r2/(RΘΦ)r^2/(R\Theta\Phi)r2/(RΘΦ).
All terms that depend on rrr then stand on one side and all terms that depend on the angles on the
other. A function of rrr can equal a function of θ\thetaθ and ϕ\phiϕ for all values of the variables
only if both are the same constant; we call it λ\lambdaλ, so that L2(ΘΦ)=λℏ2 ΘΦ\mathbf{L}^2(\Theta\Phi) = \lambda\hbar^2\,\Theta\PhiL2(ΘΦ)=λℏ2ΘΦ.
The angular equation separates once more. In (M1.2) the dependence on ϕ\phiϕ enters only through the
second derivative, so Φ′′=−m2Φ\Phi'' = -m^2\PhiΦ′′=−m2Φ with a second constant, and Φ=eimϕ\Phi = e^{im\phi}Φ=eimϕ. Since ϕ\phiϕ and
ϕ+2π\phi + 2\piϕ+2π describe the same point, ψ\psiψ must not change when ϕ\phiϕ increases by 2π2\pi2π, and this
forces mmm to be an integer. What remains is an equation for Θ\ThetaΘ. With x=cos⁡θx = \cos\thetax=cosθ, so that
d/dθ=−sin⁡θ d/dxd/d\theta = -\sin\theta\,d/dxd/dθ=−sinθd/dx and
1sin⁡θddθ(sin⁡θdΘdθ)=ddx[(1−x2)dΘdx]\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{d}{d\theta}\big(\sin\theta\frac{d\Theta}{d\theta}\big) = \frac{d}{dx}\big[(1 - x^2)\frac{d\Theta}{dx}\big]sinθ1​dθd​(sinθdθdΘ​)=dxd​[(1−x2)dxdΘ​],
it becomes the associated Legendre equation

Not every value of λ\lambdaλ is allowed, and this is where angular momentum becomes quantized. Take
m=0m = 0m=0 and try a power series Θ=∑kakxk\Theta = \sum_k a_kx^kΘ=∑k​ak​xk. Inserting it into (M1.3) and collecting the

ak+2=k(k+1)−λ(k+1)(k+2) ak,a_{k+2} = \frac{k(k+1) - \lambda}{(k+1)(k+2)}\,a_k , ak+2​=(k+1)(k+2)k(k+1)−λ​ak​,

M1.2 Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics

Section M1.1 showed that the angular solutions with m=0m = 0m=0 are polynomials, but building them
coefficient by coefficient from the recursion is clumsy. Rodrigues’ formula produces them all at once:

Pl(x)=12l l! dldxl (x2−1)l,P0=1, P1=x, P2=12(3x2−1), P3=12(5x3−3x).(M1.6)P_l(x) = \frac{1}{2^l\,l!}\,\frac{d^l}{dx^l}\,(x^2 - 1)^l , \qquad P_0 = 1,\ P_1 = x,\ P_2 = \tfrac12(3x^2 - 1),\ P_3 = \tfrac12(5x^3 - 3x). \tag{M1.6} Pl​(x)=2ll!1​dxldl​(x2−1)l,P0​=1, P1​=x, P2​=21​(3x2−1), P3​=21​(5x3−3x).(M1.6)

(x2−1) w′=2lx w(x^2 - 1)\,w' = 2lx\,w(x2−1)w′=2lxw for w=(x2−1)lw = (x^2 - 1)^lw=(x2−1)l: differentiated l+1l + 1l+1 times, it becomes Legendre’s
equation for w(l)w^{(l)}w(l) (derivation D.1). The prefactor 1/(2l l!)1/(2^l\,l!)1/(2ll!) makes Pl(1)=1P_l(1) = 1Pl​(1)=1.

A second, more physical route leads to the same polynomials and gives much more. The function
1/∣r−z^∣1/|\mathbf{r} - \hat{\mathbf{z}}|1/∣r−z^∣ is the electrostatic potential of a unit charge placed on the zzz
axis at unit distance from the origin. Away from the charge it satisfies Laplace’s equation, and it is
symmetric about the zzz axis. Separating Laplace’s equation as in §M1.1 (with E=V=0E = V = 0E=V=0) gives the
radial solutions rlr^lrl and r−l−1r^{-l-1}r−l−1, so inside the unit sphere the potential must be a sum
∑lcl rlPl(cos⁡θ)\sum_l c_l\,r^l P_l(\cos\theta)∑l​cl​rlPl​(cosθ) of solutions that are regular at the origin. On the zzz axis, where
every PlP_lPl​ equals 1, the potential is 1/(1−r)=∑lrl1/(1 - r) = \sum_l r^l1/(1−r)=∑l​rl, so all cl=1c_l = 1cl​=1. Since
∣r−z^∣=1−2rcos⁡θ+r2|\mathbf{r} - \hat{\mathbf{z}}| = \sqrt{1 - 2r\cos\theta + r^2}∣r−z^∣=1−2rcosθ+r2​, we have found the generating
function

11−2xt+t2=∑l=0∞Pl(x) tl(∣t∣<1)(M1.7)\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 2xt + t^2}} = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty}P_l(x)\,t^l \qquad (|t| < 1) \tag{M1.7} 1−2xt+t2​1​=l=0∑∞​Pl​(x)tl(∣t∣<1)(M1.7)

with t=r</r>t = r_</r_>t=r<​/r>​ and xxx the cosine of the angle between them, so (M1.7) is also the multipole

angular distribution can be expanded in YlmY_{lm}Ylm​.

M1.3 Spherical Bessel, Neumann and Hankel functions

We now turn to the radial equation of a free particle, (M1.5). For l=0l = 0l=0 it is easy: with
R=u/ρR = u/\rhoR=u/ρ it becomes u′′+u=0u'' + u = 0u′′+u=0, so u=sin⁡ρu = \sin\rhou=sinρ or cos⁡ρ\cos\rhocosρ, and the two solutions are
sin⁡ρ/ρ\sin\rho/\rhosinρ/ρ, which is finite at the origin, and cos⁡ρ/ρ\cos\rho/\rhocosρ/ρ, which diverges there. For general
lll the two solutions are the spherical Bessel function jlj_ljl​ (regular at the origin) and the
spherical Neumann function nln_lnl​ (singular). The lowest ones are

j0=sin⁡ρρ,j1=sin⁡ρρ2−cos⁡ρρ,n0=cos⁡ρρ,n1=cos⁡ρρ2+sin⁡ρρ.(M1.14)j_0 = \frac{\sin\rho}{\rho},\qquad j_1 = \frac{\sin\rho}{\rho^2} - \frac{\cos\rho}{\rho},\qquad n_0 = \frac{\cos\rho}{\rho},\qquad n_1 = \frac{\cos\rho}{\rho^2} + \frac{\sin\rho}{\rho}. \tag{M1.14} j0​=ρsinρ​,j1​=ρ2sinρ​−ρcosρ​,n0​=ρcosρ​,n1​=ρ2cosρ​+ρsinρ​.(M1.14)

Higher orders can be generated from l=0l = 0l=0 by a ladder operator, much as the excited states of the
harmonic oscillator are generated by a raising operator. If flf_lfl​ solves (M1.5), then

fl+1=−fl′+lρ fl=−ρlddρ(ρ−lfl)f_{l+1} = -f_l' + \frac{l}{\rho}\,f_l = -\rho^l\frac{d}{d\rho}\big(\rho^{-l}f_l\big) fl+1​=−fl′​+ρl​fl​=−ρldρd​(ρ−lfl​)

solves it for l+1l + 1l+1 (derivation D.4). The second form shows that fl+1/ρl+1f_{l+1}/\rho^{l+1}fl+1​/ρl+1 is
−ρ−1 d/dρ-\rho^{-1}\,d/d\rho−ρ−1d/dρ applied to fl/ρlf_l/\rho^lfl​/ρl. Applied lll times to sin⁡ρ/ρ\sin\rho/\rhosinρ/ρ and cos⁡ρ/ρ\cos\rho/\rhocosρ/ρ,
this gives Rayleigh’s formulas

jl(ρ)=(−ρ)l(1ρddρ)lsin⁡ρρ,nl(ρ)=(−ρ)l(1ρddρ)lcos⁡ρρ.(M1.15)j_l(\rho) = (-\rho)^l\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d}{d\rho}\right)^l\frac{\sin\rho}{\rho}, \qquad n_l(\rho) = (-\rho)^l\left(\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{d}{d\rho}\right)^l\frac{\cos\rho}{\rho}. \tag{M1.15} jl​(ρ)=(−ρ)l(ρ1​dρd​)lρsinρ​,nl​(ρ)=(−ρ)l(ρ1​dρd​)lρcosρ​.(M1.15)

Sign convention. As in C&H and Messiah, n0=+cos⁡ρ/ρn_0 = +\cos\rho/\rhon0​=+cosρ/ρ. Many books and
scipy.special.spherical_yn use the opposite sign: nl=−yln_l = -y_lnl​=−yl​.

The raising relation has a partner that lowers lll, fl−1=fl′+l+1ρflf_{l-1} = f_l' + \frac{l+1}{\rho}f_lfl−1​=fl′​+ρl+1​fl​. Adding the
two relations eliminates the derivative. Multiplying the lowering relation by lll, the raising
relation by l+1l + 1l+1 and subtracting eliminates fl/ρf_l/\rhofl​/ρ instead. The results are the recurrences
satisfied by both jlj_ljl​ and nln_lnl​ (written flf_lfl​ below):

fl−1+fl+1=2l+1ρ fl,(2l+1) fl′=l fl−1−(l+1) fl+1.(M1.16)f_{l-1} + f_{l+1} = \frac{2l+1}{\rho}\,f_l,\qquad (2l+1)\,f_l' = l\,f_{l-1} - (l+1)\,f_{l+1}. \tag{M1.16} fl−1​+fl+1​=ρ2l+1​fl​,(2l+1)fl′​=lfl−1​−(l+1)fl+1​.(M1.16)

The behaviour at small and large ρ\rhoρ can be read off from Rayleigh’s formulas. Near the origin, the
operator (ρ−1d/dρ)l(\rho^{-1}d/d\rho)^l(ρ−1d/dρ)l annihilates every power ρ2s\rho^{2s}ρ2s with s<ls < ls<l in the Taylor series of
sin⁡ρ/ρ\sin\rho/\rhosinρ/ρ, so the first surviving term of jlj_ljl​ is proportional to ρl\rho^lρl; for nln_lnl​, the most
singular term 1/ρ1/\rho1/ρ of cos⁡ρ/ρ\cos\rho/\rhocosρ/ρ turns into a multiple of ρ−l−1\rho^{-l-1}ρ−l−1. Far away, the term that
falls off most slowly is the one in which every derivative acts on the sine or cosine, and each
derivative shifts the phase by π/2\pi/2π/2. Working out the constants (derivation D.4) gives the limits

jl→ρ→0ρl(2l+1)!!,nl→ρ→0(2l−1)!!ρl+1,jl→ρ→∞sin⁡(ρ−lπ/2)ρ,nl→ρ→∞cos⁡(ρ−lπ/2)ρ.(M1.17)j_l \xrightarrow{\rho\to0}\frac{\rho^l}{(2l+1)!!},\quad n_l \xrightarrow{\rho\to0}\frac{(2l-1)!!}{\rho^{l+1}},\quad j_l \xrightarrow{\rho\to\infty}\frac{\sin(\rho - l\pi/2)}{\rho},\quad n_l \xrightarrow{\rho\to\infty}\frac{\cos(\rho - l\pi/2)}{\rho}. \tag{M1.17} jl​ρ→0​(2l+1)!!ρl​,nl​ρ→0​ρl+1(2l−1)!!​,jl​ρ→∞​ρsin(ρ−lπ/2)​,nl​ρ→∞​ρcos(ρ−lπ/2)​.(M1.17)

The small-ρ\rhoρ forms imply that nl/jl≈(2l−1)!! (2l+1)!!/ρ2l+1n_l/j_l \approx (2l-1)!!\,(2l+1)!!/\rho^{2l+1}nl​/jl​≈(2l−1)!!(2l+1)!!/ρ2l+1, a ratio that will
decide the stability of recurrences in §M1.8. The functions are related to the ordinary Bessel
functions of half-integer order by jl(ρ)=π/2ρ Jl+1/2(ρ)j_l(\rho) = \sqrt{\pi/2\rho}\,J_{l+1/2}(\rho)jl​(ρ)=π/2ρ​Jl+1/2​(ρ).

The factor ρl\rho^lρl near the origin has a simple physical meaning. In the radial equation the
centrifugal term l(l+1)/ρ2l(l+1)/\rho^2l(l+1)/ρ2 exceeds the “kinetic” term 1 for ρ<l(l+1)≈l+12\rho < \sqrt{l(l+1)} \approx l + \frac12ρ<l(l+1)​≈l+21​,
so this region is classically forbidden, and the regular solution only creeps up there like ρl\rho^lρl
(Fig. M1.3(a)). Classically, a particle with momentum ℏk\hbar kℏk and angular momentum ℏl\hbar lℏl passes
the origin at the impact parameter b=l/kb = l/kb=l/k and never comes closer. Partial wave lll therefore probes
only distances r≳l/kr \gtrsim l/kr≳l/k, a fact that will tell us in §M1.4 how many partial waves are needed.

In scattering we mostly use the Riccati forms j^l=ρjl\hat j_l = \rho j_lj^​l​=ρjl​ and n^l=ρnl\hat n_l = \rho n_ln^l​=ρnl​, and their
combinations h^l(±)=n^l±ij^l\hat h^{(\pm)}_l = \hat n_l \pm i\hat j_lh^l(±)​=n^l​±ij^​l​, because these solve the radial equation in the
form (M1.4), u′′+[1−l(l+1)/ρ2]u=0u'' + [1 - l(l+1)/\rho^2]u = 0u′′+[1−l(l+1)/ρ2]u=0, which has no first-derivative term. For such an equation
the Wronskian of two solutions is constant (its derivative is u1u2′′−u1′′u2=0u_1u_2'' - u_1''u_2 = 0u1​u2′′​−u1′′​u2​=0), so it can be
evaluated anywhere. At large ρ\rhoρ, (M1.17) gives j^l→sin⁡(ρ−lπ/2)\hat j_l \to \sin(\rho - l\pi/2)j^​l​→sin(ρ−lπ/2) and
n^l→cos⁡(ρ−lπ/2)\hat n_l \to \cos(\rho - l\pi/2)n^l​→cos(ρ−lπ/2), and therefore j^l′n^l−j^ln^l′=1\hat j_l'\hat n_l - \hat j_l\hat n_l' = 1j^​l′​n^l​−j^​l​n^l′​=1 (the notebook
confirms this to 12 digits). The combinations h^l(±)\hat h^{(\pm)}_lh^l(±)​ behave as e±i(ρ−lπ/2)e^{\pm i(\rho - l\pi/2)}e±i(ρ−lπ/2) far
away: they are the outgoing and incoming waves of partial wave lll, which carry the S-matrix in
Chapter 2. Remarkably, the Hankel functions have an exact, finite expansion:

h^l(+)(ρ)=ei(ρ−lπ/2)∑k=0l(l+k)!k! (l−k)!(i2ρ)k=ei(ρ−lπ/2)[1+i l(l+1)2ρ+… ].(M1.18)\hat h^{(+)}_l(\rho) = e^{i(\rho - l\pi/2)}\sum_{k=0}^{l}\frac{(l+k)!}{k!\,(l-k)!}\left(\frac{i}{2\rho}\right)^k = e^{i(\rho - l\pi/2)}\left[1 + \frac{i\,l(l+1)}{2\rho} + \dots\right]. \tag{M1.18} h^l(+)​(ρ)=ei(ρ−lπ/2)k=0∑l​k!(l−k)!(l+k)!​(2ρi​)k=ei(ρ−lπ/2)[1+2ρil(l+1)​+…].(M1.18)

To see why the series is finite, write h^l(+)=eiρw(ρ)\hat h^{(+)}_l = e^{i\rho}w(\rho)h^l(+)​=eiρw(ρ). The radial equation becomes
w′′+2iw′−l(l+1)w/ρ2=0w'' + 2iw' - l(l+1)w/\rho^2 = 0w′′+2iw′−l(l+1)w/ρ2=0, and a series w=∑kakρ−kw = \sum_k a_k\rho^{-k}w=∑k​ak​ρ−k solves it if
ak+1=i [l(l+1)−k(k+1)] ak/[2(k+1)]a_{k+1} = i\,[l(l+1) - k(k+1)]\,a_k/[2(k+1)]ak+1​=i[l(l+1)−k(k+1)]ak​/[2(k+1)]. The factor l(l+1)−k(k+1)l(l+1) - k(k+1)l(l+1)−k(k+1) vanishes at k=lk = lk=l, so the
series stops after l+1l + 1l+1 terms; solving the recursion gives the coefficients of (M1.18) (derivation

The leading correction to the asymptotic form is therefore l(l+1)/2ρl(l+1)/2\rhol(l+1)/2ρ, which Fig. M1.3(b) shows

at a matching radius rrr is accurate only if kr≫l2kr \gg l^2kr≫l2. With exact functions, which is what scatlib
uses, there is no such restriction.

M1.4 The plane-wave expansion

The incident beam of a scattering experiment is a plane wave, while the solutions we know how to
construct are partial waves of definite lll. To combine the two we need the plane wave written as a
sum of partial waves. This expansion is due to Rayleigh:

eikz=eikrcos⁡θ=∑l=0∞(2l+1) il jl(kr) Pl(cos⁡θ).(M1.19)e^{ikz} = e^{ikr\cos\theta} = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty}(2l+1)\,i^l\,j_l(kr)\,P_l(\cos\theta) . \tag{M1.19} eikz=eikrcosθ=l=0∑∞​(2l+1)iljl​(kr)Pl​(cosθ).(M1.19)

To derive it, note that eikze^{ikz}eikz solves the free Schrödinger equation (∇2+k2)ψ=0(\nabla^2 + k^2)\psi = 0(∇2+k2)ψ=0 and is
regular at the origin. It is symmetric about the zzz axis, so it can be expanded in Legendre
polynomials, eikz=∑lRl(r) Pl(cos⁡θ)e^{ikz} = \sum_l R_l(r)\,P_l(\cos\theta)eikz=∑l​Rl​(r)Pl​(cosθ). Inserting this into the free equation and using
L2Pl=l(l+1)ℏ2Pl\mathbf{L}^2P_l = l(l+1)\hbar^2P_lL2Pl​=l(l+1)ℏ2Pl​ shows that each coefficient RlR_lRl​ satisfies the free radial equation
(M1.5). It must also be regular at the origin, so Rl=Al jl(kr)R_l = A_l\,j_l(kr)Rl​=Al​jl​(kr). To find AlA_lAl​, compare the terms
proportional to (krcos⁡θ)l(kr\cos\theta)^l(krcosθ)l at small krkrkr, that is, the highest power of cos⁡θ\cos\thetacosθ that
accompanies (kr)l(kr)^l(kr)l. On the left, the Taylor series of the exponential gives
(ikrcos⁡θ)l/l!(ikr\cos\theta)^l/l!(ikrcosθ)l/l!. On the right, only the term with index lll contains (cos⁡θ)l(\cos\theta)^l(cosθ)l together
with (kr)l(kr)^l(kr)l: the lower terms contain polynomials Pl′P_{l'}Pl′​ of lower degree, and the higher terms start
with higher powers of krkrkr. That term contributes the leading power of jlj_ljl​ from (M1.17) times the
leading coefficient (2l)!/(2l l!2)(2l)!/(2^l\,l!^2)(2l)!/(2ll!2) of PlP_lPl​, which can be read off from Rodrigues’ formula.
Equating the two sides,

ill!=Al 1(2l+1)!! (2l)!2l l!2,\frac{i^l}{l!} = A_l\,\frac{1}{(2l+1)!!}\,\frac{(2l)!}{2^l\,l!^2}, l!il​=Al​(2l+1)!!1​2ll!2(2l)!​,

and with (2l)!=2l l! (2l−1)!!(2l)! = 2^l\,l!\,(2l-1)!!(2l)!=2ll!(2l−1)!! this gives Al=il(2l+1)!!/(2l−1)!!=il(2l+1)A_l = i^l(2l+1)!!/(2l-1)!! = i^l(2l+1)Al​=il(2l+1)!!/(2l−1)!!=il(2l+1).

For a wave travelling along an arbitrary direction k^\hat kk^, the polynomial Pl(cos⁡θ)P_l(\cos\theta)Pl​(cosθ) in (M1.19)
becomes Pl(k^⋅r^)P_l(\hat k\cdot\hat r)Pl​(k^⋅r^), and the addition theorem (M1.13) splits it into harmonics of the two
directions:

eik⋅r=4π∑l,mil jl(kr) Ylm∗(k^) Ylm(r^).(M1.20)e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} = 4\pi\sum_{l,m} i^l\,j_l(kr)\,Y_{lm}^*(\hat k)\,Y_{lm}(\hat r). \tag{M1.20} eik⋅r=4πl,m∑​iljl​(kr)Ylm∗​(k^)Ylm​(r^).(M1.20)

Conversely, multiplying (M1.19) by Pl(x)P_l(x)Pl​(x), with x=cos⁡θx = \cos\thetax=cosθ, integrating over xxx and using the
orthogonality (M1.9) isolates a single term and gives an integral representation of jlj_ljl​:

jl(kr)=12il∫−11eikrx Pl(x) dx.(M1.21)j_l(kr) = \frac{1}{2i^l}\int_{-1}^{1}e^{ikrx}\,P_l(x)\,dx . \tag{M1.21} jl​(kr)=2il1​∫−11​eikrxPl​(x)dx.(M1.21)

In practice the sum must be truncated, and the question is where. We saw in §M1.3 that partial wave
lll does not reach radii smaller than about l/kl/kl/k, so jl(kr)j_l(kr)jl​(kr) is negligible for l≳krl \gtrsim krl≳kr, and a
sum truncated at LLL reproduces the plane wave only inside a sphere of radius r≈L/kr \approx L/kr≈L/k.

L≈kr+3(kr)1/3L \approx kr + 3(kr)^{1/3}L≈kr+3(kr)1/3. The extra term is the width of the transition region of jlj_ljl​ near

M1.5 The Gamma function

Coulomb functions, which we need for every reaction between charged nuclei, contain the factorial of a
complex number. The Gamma function provides it. Euler’s integral defines

Γ(z)=∫0∞tz−1e−t dt(Re⁡z>0),Γ(z+1)=z Γ(z),Γ(n+1)=n!,Γ(12)=π.(M1.22)\Gamma(z) = \int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad(\operatorname{Re}z > 0), \qquad \Gamma(z+1) = z\,\Gamma(z),\quad \Gamma(n+1) = n!,\quad \Gamma(\tfrac12) = \sqrt{\pi}. \tag{M1.22} Γ(z)=∫0∞​tz−1e−tdt(Rez>0),Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z),Γ(n+1)=n!,Γ(21​)=π​.(M1.22)

The recurrence follows from an integration by parts,
∫0∞tze−t dt=[−tze−t]0∞+z∫0∞tz−1e−t dt\int_0^\infty t^ze^{-t}\,dt = \big[-t^ze^{-t}\big]_0^\infty + z\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}e^{-t}\,dt∫0∞​tze−tdt=[−tze−t]0∞​+z∫0∞​tz−1e−tdt, in which the
boundary terms vanish. With Γ(1)=1\Gamma(1) = 1Γ(1)=1 it gives Γ(n+1)=n!\Gamma(n+1) = n!Γ(n+1)=n!, and the substitution t=s2t = s^2t=s2
turns Γ(12)\Gamma(\frac12)Γ(21​) into the Gaussian integral 2∫0∞e−s2 ds=π2\int_0^\infty e^{-s^2}\,ds = \sqrt{\pi}2∫0∞​e−s2ds=π​.

The recurrence also takes Γ\GammaΓ beyond the half-plane Re⁡z>0\operatorname{Re}z > 0Rez>0. Written as
Γ(z)=Γ(z+n+1)/[z(z+1)⋯(z+n)]\Gamma(z) = \Gamma(z + n + 1)/[z(z+1)\cdots(z+n)]Γ(z)=Γ(z+n+1)/[z(z+1)⋯(z+n)], it defines Γ\GammaΓ for Re⁡z>−n−1\operatorname{Re}z > -n - 1Rez>−n−1, and
it shows simple poles at z=0,−1,−2,…z = 0, -1, -2, \dotsz=0,−1,−2,…, where one factor of the denominator vanishes. Near
z=−nz = -nz=−n the numerator tends to Γ(1)=1\Gamma(1) = 1Γ(1)=1 and the other factors give
(−n)(−n+1)⋯(−1)=(−1)n n!(-n)(-n+1)\cdots(-1) = (-1)^n\,n!(−n)(−n+1)⋯(−1)=(−1)nn!, so the residue there is (−1)n/n!(-1)^n/n!(−1)n/n!, as Fig. M1.5(a) shows.

Two identities matter for scattering. The first is the reflection formula
Γ(z) Γ(1−z)=π/sin⁡πz\Gamma(z)\,\Gamma(1 - z) = \pi/\sin\pi zΓ(z)Γ(1−z)=π/sinπz, which is proved by a contour integral of the kind discussed in
M2 §M2.4 (DLMF 5.5.3). It gives the modulus of Γ\GammaΓ on the line Re⁡z=1\operatorname{Re}z = 1Rez=1. Since
Γ(z∗)=Γ(z)∗\Gamma(z^*) = \Gamma(z)^*Γ(z∗)=Γ(z)∗, we have ∣Γ(1+iη)∣2=Γ(1+iη) Γ(1−iη)|\Gamma(1 + i\eta)|^2 = \Gamma(1 + i\eta)\,\Gamma(1 - i\eta)∣Γ(1+iη)∣2=Γ(1+iη)Γ(1−iη), and with
Γ(1+iη)=iη Γ(iη)\Gamma(1 + i\eta) = i\eta\,\Gamma(i\eta)Γ(1+iη)=iηΓ(iη) the reflection formula gives iη π/sin⁡(iπη)i\eta\,\pi/\sin(i\pi\eta)iηπ/sin(iπη). Because
sin⁡(iπη)=isinh⁡πη\sin(i\pi\eta) = i\sinh\pi\etasin(iπη)=isinhπη,

∣Γ(1+iη)∣2=πηsinh⁡πη,(M1.23)|\Gamma(1 + i\eta)|^2 = \frac{\pi\eta}{\sinh\pi\eta}, \tag{M1.23} ∣Γ(1+iη)∣2=sinhπηπη​,(M1.23)

which controls the strength of Coulomb wave functions near the origin (§M1.6). The second identity
describes large arguments. For large ∣z∣|z|∣z∣, the integrand tze−t=ezln⁡t−tt^ze^{-t} = e^{z\ln t - t}tze−t=ezlnt−t of
Γ(z+1)\Gamma(z + 1)Γ(z+1) has a sharp maximum at t=zt = zt=z, where the exponent is zln⁡z−zz\ln z - zzlnz−z and its second
derivative is −1/z-1/z−1/z. Replacing the integrand by a Gaussian around the maximum gives
Γ(z+1)≈2πz zze−z\Gamma(z + 1) \approx \sqrt{2\pi z}\,z^ze^{-z}Γ(z+1)≈2πz​zze−z. Taking the logarithm and using
ln⁡Γ(z)=ln⁡Γ(z+1)−ln⁡z\ln\Gamma(z) = \ln\Gamma(z + 1) - \ln zlnΓ(z)=lnΓ(z+1)−lnz produces the first three terms of Stirling’s series

ln⁡Γ(z)=(z−12)ln⁡z−z+12ln⁡2π+112z−1360z3+…(M1.24)\ln\Gamma(z) = \left(z - \tfrac12\right)\ln z - z + \tfrac12\ln 2\pi + \frac{1}{12z} - \frac{1}{360z^3} + \dots \tag{M1.24} lnΓ(z)=(z−21​)lnz−z+21​ln2π+12z1​−360z31​+…(M1.24)

The higher terms come from the corrections to the Gaussian approximation. The series is accurate for
∣z∣≳2|z| \gtrsim 2∣z∣≳2 away from the negative real axis.

We will meet Γ\GammaΓ of complex argument above all through the Coulomb phase shifts, the phases that a
Coulomb field adds to each partial wave (Chapter 3; §M1.6 shows where they come from):

σl=arg⁡Γ(l+1+iη),σl+1=σl+arctan⁡ηl+1.(M1.25)\sigma_l = \arg\Gamma(l + 1 + i\eta), \qquad \sigma_{l+1} = \sigma_l + \arctan\frac{\eta}{l+1}. \tag{M1.25} σl​=argΓ(l+1+iη),σl+1​=σl​+arctanl+1η​.(M1.25)

The recurrence follows from Γ(l+2+iη)=(l+1+iη) Γ(l+1+iη)\Gamma(l + 2 + i\eta) = (l + 1 + i\eta)\,\Gamma(l + 1 + i\eta)Γ(l+2+iη)=(l+1+iη)Γ(l+1+iη), because
arguments add when complex numbers are multiplied, and arg⁡(l+1+iη)=arctan⁡[η/(l+1)]\arg(l + 1 + i\eta) = \arctan[\eta/(l+1)]arg(l+1+iη)=arctan[η/(l+1)].

There is a trap in computing these phases. The principal value of the argument of a complex number
lies in (−π,π](-\pi, \pi](−π,π]. Computing σ0\sigma_0σ0​ as np.angle(gamma(1 + 1j*eta)) therefore produces jumps of
2π2\pi2π (Fig. M1.5(b)), and Γ\GammaΓ itself under- or overflows for large arguments. The safe route is the
imaginary part of scipy.special.loggamma, which is continuous. For example, σ0=3.816\sigma_0 = 3.816σ0​=3.816 at
η=5\eta = 5η=5 and 13.8013.8013.80 at η=10\eta = 10η=10. Equally safe are Stirling’s series and the recurrence in (M1.25).

M1.6 Confluent hypergeometric and Coulomb wave functions

The free solutions of §M1.3 are elementary functions. Nuclei, however, are charged, and the Coulomb
potential between them changes the radial equation at every distance, because 1/r1/r1/r falls off too
slowly to be neglected anywhere. The solutions of the Coulomb problem are confluent hypergeometric
functions, so we introduce these first. They solve Kummer’s equation

z w′′+(b−z) w′−a w=0.(M1.26)z\,w'' + (b - z)\,w' - a\,w = 0 . \tag{M1.26} zw′′+(b−z)w′−aw=0.(M1.26)

The origin is a regular singular point of this equation, so we can look for a solution as a power
series, w=∑ncnznw = \sum_n c_nz^nw=∑n​cn​zn. Inserting it and collecting the coefficient of znz^nzn gives
(n+1)(n+b) cn+1=(n+a) cn(n+1)(n+b)\,c_{n+1} = (n+a)\,c_n(n+1)(n+b)cn+1​=(n+a)cn​. With c0=1c_0 = 1c0​=1 this produces the solution regular at the origin,
Kummer’s function

M(a,b,z)=∑n=0∞(a)n(b)n znn!,(a)n=a(a+1)⋯(a+n−1),(M1.27)M(a, b, z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_n}{(b)_n}\,\frac{z^n}{n!},\qquad (a)_n = a(a+1)\cdots(a+n-1), \tag{M1.27} M(a,b,z)=n=0∑∞​(b)n​(a)n​​n!zn​,(a)n​=a(a+1)⋯(a+n−1),(M1.27)

and a second solution U(a,b,z)U(a, b, z)U(a,b,z) that decays at infinity. The Whittaker functions Mκ,μM_{\kappa,\mu}Mκ,μ​ and
Wκ,μW_{\kappa,\mu}Wκ,μ​ are the same functions in another normalization.

Now the Coulomb problem itself. Inserting U=2μZ1Z2e2/(ℏ2r)U = 2\mu Z_1Z_2e^2/(\hbar^2r)U=2μZ1​Z2​e2/(ℏ2r) into (M1.4) and dividing by
k2k^2k2, the radial equation in a Coulomb field becomes, with ρ=kr\rho = krρ=kr and the Sommerfeld parameter
η=Z1Z2e2μ/ℏ2k=Z1Z2e2/ℏv\eta = Z_1Z_2e^2\mu/\hbar^2k = Z_1Z_2e^2/\hbar vη=Z1​Z2​e2μ/ℏ2k=Z1​Z2​e2/ℏv,

u′′+[1−2ηρ−l(l+1)ρ2]u=0.(M1.28)u'' + \left[1 - \frac{2\eta}{\rho} - \frac{l(l+1)}{\rho^2}\right]u = 0 . \tag{M1.28} u′′+[1−ρ2η​−ρ2l(l+1)​]u=0.(M1.28)

The parameter η\etaη measures the strength of the Coulomb field: at the distance r=1/kr = 1/kr=1/k the Coulomb
energy is 2η2\eta2η times the kinetic energy. To solve the equation, we take out the behaviour that we
already know at both ends. Near the origin the centrifugal term dominates and the regular solution
goes as ρl+1\rho^{l+1}ρl+1; far away the solutions oscillate as e±iρe^{\pm i\rho}e±iρ. The substitution
u=ρl+1e−iρ w(2iρ)u = \rho^{l+1}e^{-i\rho}\,w(2i\rho)u=ρl+1e−iρw(2iρ) indeed turns (M1.28) into Kummer’s equation with a=l+1−iηa = l + 1 - i\etaa=l+1−iη
and b=2l+2b = 2l + 2b=2l+2 (derivation D.6). The regular Coulomb function is therefore

Fl(η,ρ)=Cl(η) ρl+1 e−iρ M(l+1−iη, 2l+2, 2iρ),Cl(η)=2l e−πη/2 ∣Γ(l+1+iη)∣(2l+1)!.(M1.29)F_l(\eta,\rho) = C_l(\eta)\,\rho^{l+1}\,e^{-i\rho}\,M(l + 1 - i\eta,\ 2l + 2,\ 2i\rho), \qquad C_l(\eta) = \frac{2^l\,e^{-\pi\eta/2}\,|\Gamma(l + 1 + i\eta)|}{(2l+1)!} . \tag{M1.29} Fl​(η,ρ)=Cl​(η)ρl+1e−iρM(l+1−iη, 2l+2, 2iρ),Cl​(η)=(2l+1)!2le−πη/2∣Γ(l+1+iη)∣​.(M1.29)

The constant ClC_lCl​ is fixed by requiring that FlF_lFl​ oscillate with unit amplitude far away, like
j^l\hat j_lj^​l​; finding it requires the asymptotic form of MMM, which is worked out in derivation D.6. The
notebook confirms (M1.29) against mpmath’s coulombf to twelve digits. The irregular function GlG_lGl​
completes the pair, and Hl(±)=Gl±iFlH^{(\pm)}_l = G_l \pm iF_lHl(±)​=Gl​±iFl​ are the Coulomb analogues of h^l(±)\hat h^{(\pm)}_lh^l(±)​. For
η=0\eta = 0η=0 they reduce exactly to j^l\hat j_lj^​l​, n^l\hat n_ln^l​ and h^l(±)\hat h^{(\pm)}_lh^l(±)​.

The long range of the Coulomb force leaves a permanent mark on the solutions far away. A simple
estimate shows what to expect. At large ρ\rhoρ the local wave number of (M1.28) is
1−2η/ρ≈1−η/ρ\sqrt{1 - 2\eta/\rho} \approx 1 - \eta/\rho1−2η/ρ​≈1−η/ρ, and the phase of a slowly varying wave grows as the
integral of the local wave number, ∫(1−η/ρ) dρ=ρ−ηln⁡ρ+const\int(1 - \eta/\rho)\,d\rho = \rho - \eta\ln\rho + \text{const}∫(1−η/ρ)dρ=ρ−ηlnρ+const. The

Fl→sin⁡θl,Gl→cos⁡θl,θl=ρ−ηln⁡2ρ−lπ2+σl.(M1.30)F_l \to \sin\theta_l,\qquad G_l \to \cos\theta_l,\qquad \theta_l = \rho - \eta\ln 2\rho - \frac{l\pi}{2} + \sigma_l . \tag{M1.30} Fl​→sinθl​,Gl​→cosθl​,θl​=ρ−ηln2ρ−2lπ​+σl​.(M1.30)

Here σl\sigma_lσl​ is the Coulomb phase (M1.25). The phase never settles to a constant: the Coulomb force
acts at all distances. At ρ=120\rho = 120ρ=120 and η=3\eta = 3η=3, the logarithmic term amounts to 16.4 rad
(Fig. M1.6©). This is why Coulomb scattering needs the special treatment of Chapter 3, and why
nuclear phase shifts are always measured relative to Coulomb functions, never to sines.

Closer in, the Coulomb barrier makes itself felt. The effective “kinetic energy” in (M1.28), the
bracket 1−2η/ρ−l(l+1)/ρ21 - 2\eta/\rho - l(l+1)/\rho^21−2η/ρ−l(l+1)/ρ2, vanishes where ρ2−2ηρ−l(l+1)=0\rho^2 - 2\eta\rho - l(l+1) = 0ρ2−2ηρ−l(l+1)=0, that is, at the

ρt=η+η2+l(l+1),(M1.31)\rho_t = \eta + \sqrt{\eta^2 + l(l+1)} , \tag{M1.31} ρt​=η+η2+l(l+1)​,(M1.31)

C02=e−πη ∣Γ(1+iη)∣2=πη e−πη/sinh⁡πηC_0^2 = e^{-\pi\eta}\,|\Gamma(1 + i\eta)|^2 = \pi\eta\,e^{-\pi\eta}/\sinh\pi\etaC02​=e−πη∣Γ(1+iη)∣2=πηe−πη/sinhπη, that is

C02(η)=2πηe2πη−1→η≫12πη e−2πη,(M1.32)C_0^2(\eta) = \frac{2\pi\eta}{e^{2\pi\eta} - 1} \xrightarrow{\eta \gg 1} 2\pi\eta\,e^{-2\pi\eta}, \tag{M1.32} C02​(η)=e2πη−12πη​η≫1​2πηe−2πη,(M1.32)

the Gamow–Sommerfeld penetration factor: C02=1.2×10−2C_0^2 = 1.2\times10^{-2}C02​=1.2×10−2 at η=1\eta = 1η=1 and

M1.7 Airy and cylindrical Bessel functions

Two more families of functions appear in later chapters, each tied to a particular physical situation.
The first arises at classical turning points, where the WKB approximation of Chapter 5 breaks down.
Near a turning point xtx_txt​, any smooth potential is approximately linear, V(x)≈E+F (x−xt)V(x) \approx E + F\,(x - x_t)V(x)≈E+F(x−xt​),
with F>0F > 0F>0 if the forbidden region lies at x>xtx > x_tx>xt​. The Schrödinger equation
−(ℏ2/2m) ψ′′+F(x−xt) ψ=0-(\hbar^2/2m)\,\psi'' + F(x - x_t)\,\psi = 0−(ℏ2/2m)ψ′′+F(x−xt​)ψ=0 then contains only one length scale,
(ℏ2/2mF)1/3(\hbar^2/2mF)^{1/3}(ℏ2/2mF)1/3, and measuring distances in this unit, z=(2mF/ℏ2)1/3(x−xt)z = (2mF/\hbar^2)^{1/3}(x - x_t)z=(2mF/ℏ2)1/3(x−xt​), turns it
into the Airy equation

d2wdz2=z w.(M1.33)\frac{d^2w}{dz^2} = z\,w . \tag{M1.33} dz2d2w​=zw.(M1.33)

Its solution that decays in the forbidden region z>0z > 0z>0 is Ai\mathrm{Ai}Ai; the other one, Bi\mathrm{Bi}Bi,
grows. Far from the turning point the solutions behave like WKB waves. For z>0z > 0z>0 the local decay
constant is z\sqrt zz​, so Ai\mathrm{Ai}Ai falls off as exp⁡(−∫z dz)=e−23z3/2\exp(-\int\sqrt z\,dz) = e^{-\frac23z^{3/2}}exp(−∫z​dz)=e−32​z3/2, with the
WKB amplitude factor z−1/4z^{-1/4}z−1/4; for z<0z < 0z<0 it oscillates. The precise constants follow from an
integral representation of Ai\mathrm{Ai}Ai by the method of stationary phase (derivation D.7). With
ξ=23∣z∣3/2\xi = \frac23|z|^{3/2}ξ=32​∣z∣3/2,

Ai(z)→z→+∞e−ξ2π z1/4,Ai(−∣z∣)→∣z∣→∞sin⁡(ξ+π/4)π ∣z∣1/4.(M1.34)\mathrm{Ai}(z) \xrightarrow{z\to+\infty}\frac{e^{-\xi}}{2\sqrt{\pi}\,z^{1/4}}, \qquad \mathrm{Ai}(-|z|) \xrightarrow{|z|\to\infty}\frac{\sin(\xi + \pi/4)}{\sqrt{\pi}\,|z|^{1/4}} . \tag{M1.34} Ai(z)z→+∞​2π​z1/4e−ξ​,Ai(−∣z∣)∣z∣→∞​π​∣z∣1/4sin(ξ+π/4)​.(M1.34)

So a decaying exponential on one side of a turning point continues as a sine with phase π/4\pi/4π/4 on the
other. This is the WKB connection formula of Chapter 5. The same function, with a different argument,
describes the intensity near a rainbow angle (Chapter 5) and the falloff of nuclear rainbows
(Chapter 7).

The second family, the cylindrical Bessel functions J0J_0J0​ and J1J_1J1​, appears whenever a plane wave is
integrated around a circle, since J0(x)=12π∫02πeixcos⁡ϕ dϕJ_0(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{ix\cos\phi}\,d\phiJ0​(x)=2π1​∫02π​eixcosϕdϕ. At high
energies the scattering is concentrated at small angles, and the amplitude can be written as an
integral over the plane of impact parameters perpendicular to the beam; the integral over the azimuth

f∝∫b db J0(qb) [… ]f \propto \int b\,db\,J_0(qb)\,[\dots]f∝∫bdbJ0​(qb)[…]. The simplest example is Fraunhofer diffraction by a black disk
of radius RRR (Chapter 7). The disk removes the incident wave over its area, and the scattered

M1.8 Evaluating special functions numerically

All these functions must eventually be computed, often for hundreds of partial waves and at many
energies. Two libraries cover almost everything in these notes. scipy.special is fast, works in
double precision and mostly takes real parameters. mpmath works in arbitrary precision and takes
complex parameters, but is slow, so it serves as the reference. The real art lies in two techniques
that both libraries use internally: choosing the direction of a recurrence, and continued fractions.

M1.8.1 The direction of a recurrence

The recurrences (M1.16) are the cheapest way to obtain jlj_ljl​ for all lll at once, but they hide a trap.
The three-term recurrence fl+1=2l+1ρfl−fl−1f_{l+1} = \frac{2l+1}{\rho}f_l - f_{l-1}fl+1​=ρ2l+1​fl​−fl−1​ is satisfied by jlj_ljl​ and by
nln_lnl​. For l>ρl > \rhol>ρ, jlj_ljl​ decreases with lll and nln_lnl​ grows: jlj_ljl​ is the minimal solution and nln_lnl​
the dominant one. If jlj_ljl​ is computed upwards from j0j_0j0​ and j1j_1j1​, each rounding error mixes in a
little nln_lnl​, and that admixture grows relative to jlj_ljl​ in proportion to nl/jln_l/j_lnl​/jl​. By §M1.3 this ratio
is (2l−1)!! (2l+1)!!/ρ2l+1(2l-1)!!\,(2l+1)!!/\rho^{2l+1}(2l−1)!!(2l+1)!!/ρ2l+1 when ρ\rhoρ is small compared with lll. At ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1 it is about
101910^{19}1019 at l=10l = 10l=10 and 4×10484\times10^{48}4×1048 at l=20l = 20l=20, so rounding errors of order 10−1610^{-16}10−16 end up far
larger than the function itself. Figure M1.8 shows the result. At ρ=1\rho = 1ρ=1 the upward recurrence is
wrong by a factor 4×1024\times10^24×102 at l=10l = 10l=10 and by 103210^{32}1032 at l=20l = 20l=20; at ρ=10\rho = 10ρ=10 the trouble
starts once lll exceeds 10.

Miller’s algorithm turns this around. Start at some NNN well beyond both lll and ρ\rhoρ with
arbitrary values (say fN+1=0f_{N+1} = 0fN+1​=0, fN=10−300f_N = 10^{-300}fN​=10−300) and run the recurrence downwards. In that
direction jlj_ljl​ is the dominant solution: as lll decreases, jlj_ljl​ grows and nln_lnl​ shrinks, so whatever
admixture of nln_lnl​ the arbitrary starting values contain dies out. Finally rescale everything with the
known value j0=sin⁡ρ/ρj_0 = \sin\rho/\rhoj0​=sinρ/ρ. The errors stay at 10−1510^{-15}10−15 for every lll. The general rule (see
Gautschi 1967) is

Run a recurrence in the direction in which the wanted solution grows.

For Coulomb functions, FlF_lFl​ decreases with lll inside the turning points and GlG_lGl​ increases. So FlF_lFl​
is computed downwards and GlG_lGl​ upwards.

M1.8.2 Continued fractions and Steed’s method

Miller’s algorithm needs a normalization at the end, and for Coulomb functions there is no simple
value, like j0=sin⁡ρ/ρj_0 = \sin\rho/\rhoj0​=sinρ/ρ, to normalize with. Steed’s method takes the normalization from the
Wronskian instead, and the starting values from continued fractions. Write the recurrences of the
Coulomb functions with Sk=k/ρ+η/kS_k = k/\rho + \eta/kSk​=k/ρ+η/k and Rk=1+η2/k2R_k = \sqrt{1 + \eta^2/k^2}Rk​=1+η2/k2​:

ul−1=Sl ul+ul′Rl,ul−1′=Sl ul−1−Rl ul;ul+1=Sl+1 ul−ul′Rl+1,ul+1′=Rl+1 ul−Sl+1 ul+1.(M1.36)u_{l-1} = \frac{S_l\,u_l + u_l'}{R_l},\quad u_{l-1}' = S_l\,u_{l-1} - R_l\,u_l; \qquad u_{l+1} = \frac{S_{l+1}\,u_l - u_l'}{R_{l+1}},\quad u_{l+1}' = R_{l+1}\,u_l - S_{l+1}\,u_{l+1}. \tag{M1.36} ul−1​=Rl​Sl​ul​+ul′​​,ul−1′​=Sl​ul−1​−Rl​ul​;ul+1​=Rl+1​Sl+1​ul​−ul′​​,ul+1′​=Rl+1​ul​−Sl+1​ul+1​.(M1.36)

Here uuu stands for FFF or GGG, and primes denote d/dρd/d\rhod/dρ; for η=0\eta = 0η=0 these are the lowering and
raising relations of §M1.3, written for the Riccati functions. Let fl=Fl′/Flf_l = F_l'/F_lfl​=Fl′​/Fl​ be the logarithmic
derivative. The upward relations give Fl+1/Fl=(Sl+1−fl)/Rl+1F_{l+1}/F_l = (S_{l+1} - f_l)/R_{l+1}Fl+1​/Fl​=(Sl+1​−fl​)/Rl+1​ and
fl+1=Rl+1Fl/Fl+1−Sl+1f_{l+1} = R_{l+1}F_l/F_{l+1} - S_{l+1}fl+1​=Rl+1​Fl​/Fl+1​−Sl+1​, and eliminating Fl+1/FlF_{l+1}/F_lFl+1​/Fl​ between them gives
fl=Sl+1−Rl+12/(Sl+1+fl+1)f_l = S_{l+1} - R_{l+1}^2/(S_{l+1} + f_{l+1})fl​=Sl+1​−Rl+12​/(Sl+1​+fl+1​). Applying the same relation to fl+1f_{l+1}fl+1​, then to
fl+2f_{l+2}fl+2​, and so on, produces a continued fraction for the logarithmic derivative, with
Tk=Sk+Sk+1T_k = S_k + S_{k+1}Tk​=Sk​+Sk+1​:

CF1:Fl′Fl=Sl+1−Rl+12Tl+1−Rl+22Tl+2−⋯.(M1.37)\text{CF1:}\qquad \frac{F_l'}{F_l} = S_{l+1} - \cfrac{R_{l+1}^2}{T_{l+1} - \cfrac{R_{l+2}^2}{T_{l+2} - \cdots}} . \tag{M1.37} CF1:Fl​Fl′​​=Sl+1​−Tl+1​−Tl+2​−⋯Rl+22​​Rl+12​​.(M1.37)

It converges to the logarithmic derivative of FFF, not of GGG, because FlF_lFl​ is the minimal solution of
the recurrence for increasing lll (a theorem of Pincherle; compare §M1.8.1). A second continued
fraction, derived from the asymptotic series of H0(+)H^{(+)}_0H0(+)​, gives the logarithmic derivative of the
outgoing Coulomb wave:

CF2:H0(+)′H0(+)=p+iq=i(1−ηρ)+iρ  α1β1+α2β2+⋯,αn=(n+iη)(n−1+iη),βn=2(ρ−η+ni).(M1.38)\text{CF2:}\qquad \frac{H_0^{(+)\prime}}{H_0^{(+)}} = p + iq = i\left(1 - \frac{\eta}{\rho}\right) + \frac{i}{\rho}\;\cfrac{\alpha_1}{\beta_1 + \cfrac{\alpha_2}{\beta_2 + \cdots}}, \qquad \alpha_n = (n + i\eta)(n - 1 + i\eta),\quad \beta_n = 2(\rho - \eta + ni). \tag{M1.38} CF2:H0(+)​H0(+)′​​=p+iq=i(1−ρη​)+ρi​β1​+β2​+⋯α2​​α1​​,αn​=(n+iη)(n−1+iη),βn​=2(ρ−η+ni).(M1.38)

Steed’s method (Barnett et al. 1974; Barnett 1981) combines them:

  1. evaluate CF1 at an order LLL inside its turning point, where FL>0F_L > 0FL​>0;
  2. recur downwards to get all FlF_lFl​, Fl′F_l'Fl′​ up to one common factor;
  3. evaluate CF2 at l=0l = 0l=0;
  4. fix the common factor with the Wronskian. Writing H0(+)=G0+iF0H_0^{(+)} = G_0 + iF_0H0(+)​=G0​+iF0​, CF2 says
    G0′+iF0′=(p+iq)(G0+iF0)G_0' + iF_0' = (p + iq)(G_0 + iF_0)G0′​+iF0′​=(p+iq)(G0​+iF0​), that is G0′=pG0−qF0G_0' = pG_0 - qF_0G0′​=pG0​−qF0​ and F0′=pF0+qG0F_0' = pF_0 + qG_0F0′​=pF0​+qG0​. Inserted
    into F′G−FG′=1F'G - FG' = 1F′G−FG′=1, these give q(F02+G02)=1q(F_0^2 + G_0^2) = 1q(F02​+G02​)=1. With γ=(F0′/F0−p)/q=G0/F0\gamma = (F_0'/F_0 - p)/q = G_0/F_0γ=(F0′​/F0​−p)/q=G0​/F0​, this
    fixes F0=±[q(1+γ2)]−1/2F_0 = \pm[q(1 + \gamma^2)]^{-1/2}F0​=±[q(1+γ2)]−1/2, and then G0=γF0G_0 = \gamma F_0G0​=γF0​ and G0′=pG0−qF0G_0' = pG_0 - qF_0G0′​=pG0​−qF0​;
  5. recur upwards for GlG_lGl​, Gl′G_l'Gl′​.

scatlib.special.coulomb_steed implements exactly these steps, using the modified Lentz algorithm for
the continued fractions. It reproduces mpmath to 10−1010^{-10}10−10 or better wherever it is meant to work. For
all l≤100l \le 100l≤100 at η=3\eta = 3η=3, ρ=25\rho = 25ρ=25 it takes 0.19 ms against 1.5 s for mpmath, a factor of 7700.
Chapters 3 and 7 need Coulomb functions for hundreds of partial waves at every energy, so this
matters.

Steed’s method has one weak spot. Deep inside the Coulomb barrier (ρ≪2η\rho \ll 2\etaρ≪2η),
q=1/(F02+G02)q = 1/(F_0^2 + G_0^2)q=1/(F02​+G02​) is tiny, and it comes out of CF2 as a small difference between numbers of order
one. Digits are lost, and on the grid of Fig. M1.9 the normalization fails outright at 45 of 651
points, all far inside the barrier. coulomb_steed estimates this loss and refuses when the error would
exceed 10−1010^{-10}10−10. The wrapper coulomb_fg then switches to mpmath, which is slow but reliable there.
Production codes switch to other methods, such as power series, in this region.

(a) Relative error against mpmath; white cells: normalization failed. (b) Number of terms needed by
CF2. The black line is the turning point ρ=2η\rho = 2\etaρ=2η. (Notebook §M1.8.)

M1.8.3 How to trust a special-function routine

A routine that returns plausible numbers is not necessarily right, so every special-function routine
should be checked against information it did not use. Three kinds are available: identities that must
hold exactly, such as Wronskians, recurrences and the addition theorem; known limits, such as small
and large arguments and the reduction of FlF_lFl​ to j^l\hat j_lj^​l​ at η=0\eta = 0η=0; and an independent
high-precision reference, such as mpmath or the DLMF tables. The test suite of scatlib uses all
three for every function in these notes.

Summary

Separating the Schrödinger equation in spherical coordinates reduces a central-force problem to
angular and radial equations, and the requirement that the wave function be finite on the whole sphere
quantizes the separation constant to l(l+1)l(l+1)l(l+1). The angular solutions are the Legendre polynomials and
the spherical harmonics. A single generating function, the potential of a point charge, supplies their
recurrence, orthogonality, parity and normalization; the addition theorem expresses the fact that
rotations mix the harmonics of one lll only among themselves; and for large lll the polynomials become
modulated cosines with the effective wave number l+12l + \frac12l+21​. The free radial solutions jlj_ljl​ and nln_lnl​,
and their Riccati and Hankel forms, follow from sin⁡ρ\sin\rhosinρ and cos⁡ρ\cos\rhocosρ by a ladder operator. They stay
small inside ρ≈l\rho \approx lρ≈l, where the centrifugal barrier keeps partial wave lll away, and approach
their asymptotic forms with a correction l(l+1)/2ρl(l+1)/2\rhol(l+1)/2ρ; Rayleigh’s expansion of a plane wave in these
partial waves therefore converges once LLL exceeds krkrkr by a transition width,
L≈kr+3(kr)1/3L \approx kr + 3(kr)^{1/3}L≈kr+3(kr)1/3. The Gamma function supplies the factorials of complex numbers that the
Coulomb problem needs. Its reflection formula gives ∣Γ(1+iη)∣2=πη/sinh⁡πη|\Gamma(1+i\eta)|^2 = \pi\eta/\sinh\pi\eta∣Γ(1+iη)∣2=πη/sinhπη, and the
Coulomb phases σl=arg⁡Γ(l+1+iη)\sigma_l = \arg\Gamma(l+1+i\eta)σl​=argΓ(l+1+iη) must be computed from Im⁡ln⁡Γ\operatorname{Im}\ln\GammaImlnΓ,
never from a principal-value argument. Coulomb functions are confluent hypergeometric functions: their
phase grows as ηln⁡2ρ\eta\ln 2\rhoηln2ρ without limit, because the force never stops acting, and their penetration
factor C02≈2πη e−2πηC_0^2 \approx 2\pi\eta\,e^{-2\pi\eta}C02​≈2πηe−2πη is the Gamow factor of M0. Airy functions describe turning
points and rainbows, and J0J_0J0​ and J1J_1J1​ describe eikonal amplitudes and diffraction. Computing all of
this reliably rests on two ideas: a recurrence must run in the direction in which the wanted solution
grows, and Steed’s method combines two continued fractions, the recurrences and a Wronskian into an
algorithm that is fast and accurate everywhere except deep inside the Coulomb barrier.

Several results above were derived only in outline, so as not to interrupt the argument. This section
gives the complete algebra, in the order in which the results appear in the chapter.
